title: Pancakes on Friday
text:
It is Friday evening. The Arslan family is in the kitchen. Tonight, they make pancakes for dinner.

"Who wants to help?" asks their father. "Me!" says Zeynep. "Me too!" says her little brother Can.

Their father makes the batter. Then Zeynep cooks the pancakes in a pan. Can puts chocolate on them. Then he puts more chocolate. And more chocolate.

"Can, that is a lot of chocolate!" says Zeynep. "I love chocolate," says Can. "Chocolate is the best."

Their mother laughs. "Let's put some fruit on them too," she says. So Zeynep adds bananas and strawberries. Can does not like bananas. He puts them on his sister's plate.

After twenty minutes, the kitchen smells very good. "Are they ready?" asks Can. "Yes, they are ready," says their father.

The family sits at the table. The pancakes are hot and sweet. Can eats four pancakes. "These are the best pancakes in the world," he says.

title: The Tree in the School Play
text:
This is Nina. She is eight. Her class has a play in June. Every child has a part.

"Who wants to be the queen?" asks Ms Bell. Everybody puts up their hand. The part of the queen goes to Ella. The king is a boy called Tom. And Nina? She is a tree.

"A tree?" says Nina at home. "Trees do not talk. Trees do not move." "A tree is important too," says her mother.

She goes to every practice. She stands still for a long time. She watches the other children. Soon she knows all their words.

On the day of the play, Ella is ill. She cannot come. "What now?" says Ms Bell. "Who knows the queen's words?" "I do," says a small voice at the back. It is the tree!

That evening, Nina is the queen. She does not forget one word. Her mother claps and claps.

"Next year, I want to be a tree," says Nina. "Trees learn everything!"

title: A Fish Called Bubbles
text:
This is Ayşe. She is seven years old. She has a small goldfish. His name is Bubbles. He lives in a round bowl in the living room.

Every morning, she gives him a little food. "Good morning, Bubbles," she says. The little fish swims to the top.

One morning, she looks at the bowl. The water is not clean. It is green. "Dad!" she shouts. "The water is green!" "Don't worry," says her dad. "We can clean it together."

First, he puts Bubbles in a cup of water. She washes the bowl. Then her dad puts in fresh water. "Can Bubbles go home now?" asks Ayşe. "Not yet," says her dad. "This water is too cold. Let's wait one hour."

After one hour, Bubbles goes back into the bowl. He swims fast. "He is happy," says Ayşe. "Yes," says her dad. "Clean water every week, OK?" "OK, Dad. Every Saturday!"

title: My New Class
text:

How are you? I am fine. I am at my new school now. It is big, and the building is yellow.

title: A Puzzle and a Cold
text:
My name is Emre, and I am ten. On Mondays, I usually go to school by bus. But this Monday, I stay at home. I have a cold.

My nose is red, and my head hurts. I am in bed with a cup of tea. I am bored.

My grandfather comes into my room. "Come, Emre," he says. "Let's do something quiet." He brings an old box from his room. In the box, there is a big puzzle. It has one thousand pieces. The picture is a ship on the sea.

We put the puzzle on the kitchen table. First, we find the edges. Then we do the ship. My mother makes soup for me.

In the afternoon, my friend Can calls. "Do you want to play football tomorrow?" "No, thanks," I say. "I want to finish my puzzle."

At nine o'clock, it is ready. But one piece is missing!

Maybe a cold is not so bad.

title: A Cake for Kerem
text:
Today is Kerem's birthday. His sister Elif wants to make a cake for him.

"What cake does Kerem like?" she asks their mother on the phone. "Chocolate, of course," says her mother. "He loves chocolate."

Elif finds a recipe. She buys eggs, sugar, flour and a lot of chocolate. She works all afternoon. The kitchen is a mess, but the cake looks beautiful.

At seven, Kerem arrives. "Surprise!" says Elif. "Happy birthday!" Kerem looks at the cake. He is happy, but he does not eat. "What's wrong?" asks Elif. "I love it, Elif," he says. "But I don't eat sugar this month. My doctor says no."

Elif is sad for one second. Then she laughs. "OK. Then I can eat your piece!" "No, no," says Kerem. "One small piece. It is my birthday!"

They eat the cake together. It is very good.

title: Birds in My Notebook
text:
I am Hasan, and I am twelve. My hobby is drawing birds.

I started last spring. One morning, a small bird sat on our balcony. It was brown, with a red face. I took my pencil and drew it. The drawing was not very good, but I liked it.

Now I have a special notebook. It is only for birds. After school, I sit on the balcony for twenty minutes. I wait, I watch and I draw.

There are many birds in my city. I see pigeons every day. They are easy to draw. Seagulls are big and loud. Sparrows are small and fast, so they are difficult.

My father buys me a book about birds. Now I know their names in English and in Turkish.

My notebook has forty-one birds now. But I still like the first one most. It is the little brown bird with the red face.

title: Elif's Lemonade
text:
Every summer, Elif makes lemonade for her friends. It is easy and cheap. Here is her recipe.

You need four lemons and five glasses of cold water. You also need a cup of sugar. Some ice and mint leaves are nice too.

First, wash the lemons. Cut them in half. Then squeeze them into a big jug.

Next, add the sugar. Add a little warm water and mix well. Sugar likes warm water!

Then add the cold water. Mix again. Now taste it. Is it too sour? Add more sugar.

Put the jug in the fridge for one hour. Before you drink it, add ice and mint leaves.

That's it! Your lemonade is ready. Give a glass to your family or friends.

title: Meet Pamuk
text:
This week, our school newspaper talks to Defne. She is in class 5B. She has a dog.

Reporter: Hello, Defne. Tell us about your dog.
Defne: Her name is Pamuk. That means "cotton" in English. She is small and white, like cotton. She is four years old.

Reporter: Where does Pamuk sleep?
Defne: In a basket next to my bed. But at night, she often jumps on my bed!

Reporter: What does she eat?
Defne: Dog food, and sometimes carrots or apples. She loves cheese, but I only give her a little.

Reporter: Who walks her?
Defne: My father and I. We walk her twice a day. We go in the morning and in the evening. In the evening, she plays with dogs in the park.

Reporter: Is a dog a lot of work?
Defne: Yes! When it rains, she gets very dirty. Then we wash her.

Reporter: Any advice for our readers?
Defne: A dog is not a toy. It is a friend for many years.

title: Sam's Washing Machine
text:
It is Sunday morning. Sam puts his clothes in the washing machine. He presses the button. Nothing happens.

He presses it again. Nothing. So he calls his friend Kerem. "Kerem, my washing machine does not work. Can you help me?" "Sam, I work with computers. I do not fix washing machines!" "Please. You know machines." Kerem laughs. "OK. I can come at eleven."

At eleven, Kerem arrives. He looks at the machine. He opens the door and closes it. He presses the button. Nothing. "Is it on?" asks Kerem. "Of course it is on," says Sam. Kerem looks behind the machine. Then he laughs. "Sam, look. The plug is not in the wall."

Sam's face goes red. He puts the plug in. The machine starts. "Thank you, Kerem," he says. "Lunch is on me." "Good," says Kerem. "I want a very big lunch."

title: Summer Nights on the Balcony
text:
I live in Adana with my family. In summer, Adana is very hot. In July, it is often near forty degrees. During the day, we stay inside. We close the curtains and turn on the fan.

But the evenings are wonderful. After dinner, we all go out to the balcony. My mother brings watermelon and cold water. My father plays old songs on his phone. My little brother sleeps there on a mattress.

We sit and talk. Our neighbours sit outside too. We say "good evening" to them. Sometimes they give us figs from their garden.

At midnight, the air is cooler. I look at the sky and see some stars.

Winter in Adana is short and rainy. It is not bad. But every year, I wait for summer. I love our balcony nights.

title: Two Blue Notebooks
text:
Two boys, Jack and Ali, are in the same class. They sit next to each other. They have the same blue notebook.

On Monday morning, the teacher asks for the homework. "Where is your homework, Jack?" So Jack opens his notebook. The pages are empty. "I do not understand," he says. "I did it last night!" "Everybody says that," says Mr Kaya.

Then Ali looks at his notebook. There is maths homework in it. But it is not his writing. "Mr Kaya," he says. "I think this is Jack's notebook." "Yes! That is my homework!" says Jack. "So where is your homework, Ali?" asks Mr Kaya. Now Ali looks at the empty notebook. He is quiet for a moment. "I... I forgot it," he says.

Everybody laughs, even Mr Kaya. "OK, Ali. Bring it tomorrow. And Jack, write your name on your notebook!"

title: Tomatoes on My Balcony
text:
My name is Deniz. I live in a flat in İstanbul. I do not have a garden. But I have a small balcony. And on my balcony, I grow tomatoes.

In March, I buy small tomato plants from the market. They are very small and green. I put them in big pots with good soil.

Every morning before work, I water them. In April and May, they grow fast. In June, I see the first little flowers. They are yellow.

In July, the first tomatoes come. At first they are green. Then, day by day, they turn red. I wait and wait.

Finally, in August, I pick the first red tomato. I wash it and eat it with a little salt. It is warm from the sun, and it tastes great. Shop tomatoes are never like this!

Next year, I want to grow peppers too.

title: A Sleepy Tortoise
text:
Sam has a pet tortoise. Her name is Lady Grey. She is twenty years old. She is from London, like Sam.

In summer, his tortoise is very busy. She walks around the small garden. She eats lettuce, flowers and strawberries.

But in October, the weather gets cold. Now Lady Grey eats less. She does not move much. One day, Sam's sister Mia visits. "Sam, is your tortoise ill?" she asks. "No, she is fine," says Sam. "She is sleepy. Many tortoises sleep in winter." "For how long?" "About three months." "Three months! I want that too," says Mia.

Sam puts Lady Grey in a box with soft paper. He puts the box in a cool, quiet room. "Good night, Lady Grey," he says. "See you in spring."

In March, the sun is warm again. The tortoise opens her eyes. She walks out of the box. Sam gives her some strawberries. Spring is here!

title: A Library Card
text:
Sam wanted to read more in Turkish. On Saturday morning, he went to the city library. The building was old, but the reading room was bright and quiet.

At the desk, a young woman smiled at him. "Good morning. Can I help you?"

"Yes, please. I'd like a library card," Sam said slowly.

"Of course. Do you have your ID card with you?"

"I have my residence permit. Is that OK?"

"Yes, that's fine. Please fill in this form."

Sam wrote his name, address and phone number. Then the woman took his photo with a small camera.

"How many books can I borrow?" Sam asked.

"Five books for three weeks. You can renew them online, too."

"Is the card free?"

"Yes, it's free for everyone in the city."

Sam was happy. He walked between the shelves and found the children's section. "I think these books are right for my Turkish," he said and laughed.

He chose two picture books and a short novel. At the desk, the woman stamped each book.

"Don't be late," she said. "We send a message three days before the return date."

That evening, Sam read the first picture book on his balcony. He understood almost every word.

title: Hands in the Clay
text:
Deniz spent every day at a desk, planning deliveries. In March, Deniz wanted a hobby away from screens. A colleague suggested a pottery class on Tuesday evenings.

The room was small and warm. There were six students and a teacher called Nermin. There was clay on her hands and her apron.

"Tonight, we'll make a simple bowl," she said. "Don't worry about mistakes. Clay is patient."

First, Deniz pressed the clay into a ball. Then Nermin turned on the wheel.

"Keep your hands wet and your arms still," she said.

It looked easy when Nermin did it. But Deniz's clay moved to one side. Then the bowl fell down completely.

"Oh no," Deniz said. "It looks like a pancake."

The teacher laughed. "Everyone makes one in the first lesson. Try again, but slower this time."

The second bowl was small and a bit uneven, but it stood up.

Nermin said, "Now it needs to dry for a week. Then it goes into a very hot oven."

"Can I take it home after that?" Deniz asked.

"Of course. It's yours."

Two weeks later, Deniz took the bowl home. It wasn't perfect. But now it sits on the breakfast table every morning, full of olives.

title: A Summer at the Animal Shelter
text:
Last summer, I was sixteen and I had a lot of free time. My mother said, "Do something useful." So I became a volunteer at the animal shelter near our town.

The shelter has about sixty dogs and thirty cats. Most of them came from the streets. Some were sick or hurt when they arrived.

I went there every Saturday and Sunday morning. My first job was not exciting. I cleaned the cages and washed the food bowls. It smelled terrible, and I often wanted to go home.

After two weeks, the manager, Gül Hanım, gave me a new job. I walked the dogs. Every dog was different. Some pulled hard. Others were afraid of cars and noise.

One old dog, Karabaş, never came out of his cage. He was afraid of people. So every day I sat next to his cage and read a book aloud. In August, he finally took food from my hand.

In September, a family adopted Karabaş. I was happy, but I cried a little too.

Now I still go to the shelter every Sunday. One day, I want to be a vet.

title: The Noisy Bike
text:
Zeynep's bike made a bad noise on the way to school. Then the chain came off. After school, she pushed the bike to a small repair shop on Çınar Street.

An old man looked up from a wheel. "Good afternoon. What's the problem?"

"My chain came off, and the bike makes a funny noise," Zeynep said.

The man turned the pedals slowly. "Ah, I see. The chain is very dry. When did you last oil it?"

"Oil it? Never, I think."

He laughed. "A chain is like a person. It needs a drink sometimes."

"Can you fix it today? I need it tomorrow."

"Of course. Come back in an hour. The brakes need some work, too."

"How much will it cost?"

"Let's say two hundred lira. If I need a new part, I'll call you first."

She sat in the park and did her homework. After an hour, she came back. Her bike was clean and quiet.

"Here's a small bottle of oil," the man said. "Put a few drops on the chain every month. Then you won't need me so often."

"But I like your shop," Zeynep said with a smile.

"Then come and say hello. Just not with a broken bike!"

title: A Train to Selçuk
text:
Last April, my husband and I wanted a cheap weekend away. We live in İzmir, so we didn't need a car or a plane. We took a train from Basmane station to Selçuk. The journey took about an hour and a half.

The town of Selçuk is small and quiet. In spring, storks build nests on an old stone aqueduct. From our hotel window, we counted eleven nests!

On Saturday morning, we walked up to the old castle on the hill above the town. From the top, we could see the whole valley. The castle walls were my favourite part.

In the afternoon, we took a minibus up into the hills to Şirince. It's a village with white houses and narrow streets. Many shops sell fruit wine and olive oil soap. We bought some soap for my mother.

On Sunday morning it rained. We stayed in the hotel, drank tea and wrote postcards.

We came home on the evening train. It was a short trip, but we want to go back in autumn.

title: Greetings from Ljubljana
text:
Subject: Greetings from Ljubljana!

Hi Elif,

I'm writing from a little coffee shop next to the river in Ljubljana. It's the capital of Slovenia, but it feels like a small town. I'm here for three days for work, and today is my free day.

Most of the old town centre has no cars, so it's very quiet. People walk or ride bikes in the streets. This morning I rented a bike for a few euros.

There are many bridges over the river. My favourite is the Dragon Bridge. It has four big green dragons on it! People told me the dragon is the symbol of the city.

After lunch, I took a funicular up the hill to the castle. It's like a small train that climbs. The view from the top was amazing. I could see red roofs and green mountains far away.

The food is good, too. Yesterday I tried a local sausage with potatoes. It was delicious.

Tomorrow I fly back to İstanbul. I'm bringing you a little dragon for your desk!

See you on Saturday?
Mia

title: A Young Chess Champion
text:
Ece Tunç is twelve years old. Last month she won the town's junior chess tournament. We met her at the community centre, where the chess club meets every Saturday.

Reporter: Ece, congratulations! How did you start playing chess?

Ece: My grandfather taught me when I was six. We played every evening after dinner.

Reporter: Do you still play with him?

Ece: Yes, but now I win most games. He isn't very happy about that!

Reporter: Why did you join the club?

Ece: I wanted new people to play with. At the club, there are children and adults. Everyone plays with everyone.

Reporter: How much do you practise?

Ece: About an hour a day. I also solve chess puzzles on my tablet.

Reporter: What was the hardest moment in the tournament?

Ece: The final game. It took two hours. My hands were cold, and I couldn't eat my sandwich.

Reporter: What advice do you have for beginners?

Ece: Don't be afraid to lose. I lost hundreds of games. Every time, I learned something new.

Reporter: And what's next?

Ece: The regional tournament in April. I'm a bit nervous, but I'm excited too.

title: One Player Short
text:
Every Thursday evening, Kerem plays five-a-side football with people from his office. They rent a small pitch near the metro station for one hour.

This Thursday, there was a problem. Only nine people came.

"We need ten," said Burcu, the team captain. "Who can we call?"

"My neighbour plays sometimes," Kerem said. "But he is away this week."

Just then, a tall man walked past the pitch with a sports bag.

"Excuse me!" Burcu shouted. "Do you want to play with us? We need one more player."

The man stopped. "Really? I'm waiting for my friends, but they're late. OK, why not?"

His name was Ali, and he was very fast. He played on Kerem's team. In twenty minutes, he scored three goals.

"Who is this guy?" asked Ozan from the other team. "Is he a professional?"

Ali laughed. "No, I'm a dentist. But I played for my university."

At the end, Kerem's team won seven to four. Everyone shook hands.

"Come again next Thursday," Kerem said. "We need a fast player like you."

"I'll come," Ali said. "But next week I'll play on the other team. Then it's fair."

"Thank you!" Ozan said. "Finally, some good news for us!"

title: How to Plan a Game Night
text:
A game night is a cheap and fun evening with friends. Here are some simple steps.

First, choose a date and invite people. Four to six players is a good number. With more people, the games become too long.

Next, choose the games. Have one easy game and one longer board game. Easy card games are good at the start, because people are still arriving. You can ask your friends to bring their favourite games, too.

Read the rules before the evening. Nothing is more boring than reading a long rule book for thirty minutes. If the rules are difficult, watch a short video.

Prepare simple food. Choose food that people can eat with one hand. Crisps, nuts or small sandwiches are good. Keep drinks on a different table. A glass of juice can ruin a game board in one second!

Be a good host. Explain the rules slowly and help new players. Remember, the aim is to have fun, not to win every game.

Finally, finish on time, because many people work the next day. Before everyone leaves, take a photo with the winner. Then choose a date for the next game night.

title: How to Save for a Summer Holiday
titleTr: Yaz tatili için nasıl para biriktirilir?
text:
Do you want a holiday next summer, but you never have enough money? Try these easy ideas.

First, decide where you want to go and find out the cost. Write the number on a piece of paper. For example, "Kaş, one week: 45,000 lira." Put the paper on your fridge.

Next, divide it by the number of months before your holiday. If you have ten months, you need to save 4,500 lira a month. Now the big number looks smaller.

Then open a separate bank account only for the holiday. On payday, move the money into this account first. Don't wait until the end of the month. By then, the money is usually gone.

Look at your small daily costs, too. A café coffee every morning can cost over a thousand lira a month. Make coffee at home three days a week. Then put the difference in a jar.

Finally, check your progress every month. When you reach half of your goal, celebrate a little. But don't spend the holiday money!

title: The Green Armchair
text:
Mia needed an armchair for her new flat. New ones were too expensive. So she went to a second-hand furniture shop near her home.

The shop was full of old tables, lamps and mirrors. In the corner, she saw a green armchair.

"How much is this armchair?" she asked.

The owner, a man with a grey moustache, looked up from his newspaper. "That one? Three thousand lira."

"Three thousand? But there's a small hole here, on the arm."

"That's not a hole. That's history," he said with a smile. "It's from the 1970s."

Mia sat in the chair. It was very comfortable. "I can pay two thousand," she said.

"Two thousand is too little. Two thousand six hundred."

"Two thousand two hundred, and I'll carry it home myself."

The man laughed. "Do you live near here?"

"Yes, two streets away. On the third floor."

"Third floor, without a lift?"

"Without a lift," Mia said.

"OK, OK. Two thousand four hundred, and my son carries it for you. Deal?"

"Deal!" Mia said, and she shook his hand.

That evening, Mia sat in her green armchair with a cup of tea. The small hole was still there. But now it was part of her history, too.

title: Half a Size Too Small
text:
Last Saturday, Aylin bought a pair of white trainers. On Monday she wore them to work. By one o'clock, her feet hurt badly. The shoes were half a size too small.

On Tuesday, she took them back to the shop. She had the box and the receipt in her bag.

"Hello. I bought these trainers on Saturday, but they're too small," she said.

The shop assistant looked at the shoes. "Did you wear them outside?"

"Only once, for a few hours. I'm sorry."

"I see. The bottoms are a little dirty. We can't give you your money back for worn shoes."

She felt disappointed. "So I can't return them?"

"You can't return them, but you can change them. Would you like a bigger size?"

"Yes, please! Size thirty-nine."

The assistant went to the back of the shop. After a few minutes she came back. "I'm sorry, we don't have thirty-nine in white. We have it in grey."

Aylin tried on the grey pair. They fitted perfectly.

"Actually, grey is better," Aylin said. "White shoes get dirty so quickly."

The assistant laughed. "That's true. Next time, walk around the shop for a few minutes first."

"Good idea," Aylin said. "I learned that lesson the hard way."

title: Hundreds of Kites over the Beach
text:
More than two thousand people came to Yeniköy's first kite festival on Sunday. The festival was on the long beach south of the town.

The weather was perfect. There was a strong wind and almost no clouds. By twelve o'clock, hundreds of kites in many colours were flying in the sky. Some were very big. One kite looked like a whale and was twelve metres long.

The town council organised the event with a local school. Before the festival, teachers showed children how to make kites. They used paper, wood and string. More than three hundred children made their own kites.

"My kite is a fish," said nine-year-old Kaan. "It went up very high, but then it fell into the sea!"

There was also food, music and a competition for the most beautiful kite. First prize went to Defne Sarı, eleven, for a red and yellow bird.

The mayor said the festival was a big success. "We want to do it every year," he said. "Next year, we hope to invite kite clubs from other countries."

After the festival, volunteers collected forty bags of rubbish from the beach.

title: Wishes on a Rose Bush
text:
In my town, Edirne, the night of 5 May is very special. It's Hıdırellez, a spring festival. Old stories say that two holy men meet on earth on this day. Their names are Hızır and İlyas. Many people say summer begins after this night.

When I was a child, my grandmother prepared me for the festival. In the afternoon, we wrote our wishes on small pieces of paper. I always wished for a bicycle. My older sister wished for good exam results.

In the evening, we went to the rose bush in our garden. We tied our wishes to its branches with red ribbon. My grandmother said, "Don't tell anyone your wish. If you tell, it won't come true."

Later, the whole street went to the park by the river. There was music, dancing and a big fire. Young people jumped over the fire, and everyone clapped. I was too small, so I watched from my father's shoulders.

Early the next morning, we took our wishes from the rose bush. Some families put them in the river.

Did my wishes come true? Well, I got the bicycle when I was nine. So maybe the rose bush listened!

title: Fireworks and Cold Hands
text:
Subject: Fireworks and cold hands

Hi Sam,

How are you, cousin? How is İstanbul? Here in London it's cold and grey, but last night was Bonfire Night!

Do you remember it? Every year on the fifth of November, there are fireworks and big fires. It's about a man called Guy Fawkes. In 1605, he and his friends wanted to blow up the Houses of Parliament. They failed, and people lit fires to celebrate. That was more than four hundred years ago, but we still do it.

This year I took the kids to the park near my mum's house. It was crowded, and we stood in the mud for an hour. But the fireworks were wonderful. Little Leo held my hand and shouted "Wow!" at every one.

We had toffee apples, like when we were children. Mine was so sticky! And Maya wrote her name in the air with a sparkler.

My mum says hello. She asks, "When is Sam coming home for Christmas?" So, when are you coming?

Love,
Lucy

P.S. Do people in Turkey have a night like this?

title: Plan B on a Rainy Saturday
text:
On Friday evening, Elif called Mia.

"Hi! Do you have plans for Saturday?"

"Not really. I want to get out of the house. Any ideas?"

"Let's walk along the coast. Then we can have fish for lunch."

"Perfect. What time?"

"Ten o'clock at the ferry station?"

"OK, see you there!"

On Saturday morning, Mia opened the curtains. It was raining heavily. She checked the weather app. There was rain all day, and a strong wind.

She called Elif. "Have you looked outside?"

"Yes," Elif said sadly. "Our walk is a bad idea now."

"So what do we do? I don't want to stay at home."

"What about bowling? There's a bowling centre in the new shopping centre."

"Bowling? I haven't played for ten years!"

"Neither have I. That's why it'll be fun."

They met at eleven. Their first games were terrible. Again and again, Mia's ball went into the side. Elif laughed so much that she had to sit down.

But in the third game, Mia knocked down all ten pins. She jumped and shouted. The people next to them clapped.

"You know," Mia said later, "I'm happy it rained today."

"Me too," said Elif. "But next week, the sea!"

title: New Bus Line to the Hospital
text:
A new bus line will start next Monday. It will connect the east side of the city with the State Hospital. The number of the new line is 47.

Until now, people from the east side needed two buses for the hospital. The journey often took more than an hour. With line 47, it will take about twenty-five minutes.

On weekdays, the buses will run every fifteen minutes. They will start at six in the morning and stop at eleven at night. At weekends, they will run every thirty minutes. Passengers can pay with their city card, as on other lines.

The new buses are electric and very quiet. They also have more space for wheelchairs and pushchairs.

Many people are happy about the change. "My mother visits the hospital every week," said Hülya Demir, 52. "Now she can go alone. Before, I always had to drive her."

But some shop owners on Atatürk Street are not happy. The new bus stop is in front of their shops. "Where will our customers park?" asked one café owner.

The city council has an answer. Next year, there will be a car park behind the street.

title: Music on the Street
text:
Every evening, a young man plays the guitar near the ferry station. Crowds stop and listen. His name is Emre Kaya, and he is twenty-six. Mia talked to him after his show.

Mia: How long have you played in the street?

Emre: For about three years. Before that, I worked in a bank.

Mia: Why did you leave the bank?

Emre: I was bored. Music was always my real love. One day I took my guitar to the street, and people listened.

Mia: Do you earn enough money?

Emre: Some days, yes. On a good Saturday, I earn more than in a day at the bank. On a rainy day, I earn nothing.

Mia: What do people usually ask for?

Emre: Old Turkish songs. Tourists often ask for the Beatles, too!

Mia: What's the hardest part?

Emre: The weather, and sometimes the noise. Once a man asked me to stop because his baby was sleeping. So I played very quietly.

Mia: What's your best memory?

Emre: Last summer, an old couple danced in front of me. It was their fiftieth wedding anniversary. Everyone clapped.

Mia: What are your plans?

Emre: I want to record my own songs. But I'll always play in the street. Here, I meet real people.

title: Who Pays What?
text:
Four friends, Can, Damla, Arda and Nehir, had dinner at a restaurant. They wanted to celebrate the end of their exams. At the end of the evening, the waiter brought the bill.

"Two thousand four hundred lira," said Can. "So it's six hundred each. Easy."

"Wait a minute," said Nehir. "I only had a salad and water. That's about three hundred lira."

"And I had no dessert," said Arda.

Damla laughed. "OK, let's do it properly. Give me the bill."

She looked at the list carefully. "Can, you had the meat dish, a juice and the chocolate cake. That's seven hundred and fifty."

"Fine," Can said. "I was hungry."

"Then Arda, the fish and two lemonades. That's five hundred and twenty. Then Nehir, salad and water, three hundred and ten. And my sandwich and tea are four hundred and eighty."

Then Arda checked on his phone. "That's two thousand and sixty. What about the rest?"

"That's the bread for the table and the service charge," Damla said. "We can split it four ways. That's eighty-five each."

"You're like a bank," said Nehir with a smile.

"My mother is an accountant," Damla answered. "I learned from her."

Can paid by card, and everyone sent him their share by phone.
